title: The One It Is Done To

lessons.title: -ஐ (-ai) — your second case ending
lessons.gloss: the accusative suffix -ai, which marks the one the verb is done to

segments.text: Your first case ending was -உக்கு, and what it taught was bigger than its meaning: English puts a word in front, Tamil sticks a piece on the back.
Here is the second piece, and it goes on the same end.
-ஐ — -ai — marks the one the verb is done to.

A sentence can have two people in it, and something has to say which of them is doing and which is being done to. English uses position: the teacher saw the child and the child saw the teacher are built from the same three words and mean opposite things, and the only signal is the order.
Tamil marks the one being done to, and then the order stops carrying the weight:
நான் அவரை நினைக்கிறேன் nāṉ avarai ninaikkiṟēṉ — "I think of them".
அவர் became அவரை. Nothing else moved. The verb you already know from the thinking chapter did not change, and nāṉ is still optional because the -ēṉ on the end is already saying "I".

blocks.title: Grammar Lens: where the two endings sit

utterances: the word: அவர். + ending: அவர்உக்கு becomes அவருக்கு. what it says: to them, for them.
the word: அவர். + ending: அவர்ஐ becomes அவரை. what it says: them, as the one it is done to.

segments.text: Two endings, one place to put them, and the noun underneath is the same word both times. A case ending in Tamil is a seam you can see, which is the thing the dative chapter said was the biggest structural fact about the language — and this is the second piece of evidence for it rather than a new idea.

segments.text: What does -ஐ (-ai) mark? (The one the verb is done to.) Where does it go? (On the end of the word, like every Tamil case ending.) What is avar as the one it is done to? (Avarai.) And what does English use instead of an ending here? (Position — which word comes first.)

lessons.title: என்னை / உன்னை (eṉṉai / uṉṉai) — the body you already changed once
lessons.gloss: me and you as the one it is done to, standing on the same changed body the dative already used

needs: your eyes, because the lesson points at something written down

segments.text: Say "to me". Then say the word for "I" on its own.
They do not look like each other, and the dative chapter told you why: the pronoun changes its body before an ending lands on it.

blocks.title: You'll want to know: என்னை and உன்னை

segments.text: என்னை — eṉṉai — me, as the one it is done to உன்னை — uṉṉai — you, as the one it is done to.
These cost you nothing new. You changed nāṉ into eṉ- to build enakku chapters ago. That changed body is the same one -ஐ (-ai) lands on:

headers: the one it is done to
utterances: the word: நான் nāṉ — I. to / for: எனக்கு enakku. the one it is done to: என்னை eṉṉai.
the word: நீ nī — you. to / for: உனக்கு unakku. the one it is done to: உன்னை uṉṉai.

segments.text: Read down the middle column and then down the right one. The left part of each word never changes once you have it. Learning the body is the work; the endings are the cheap part, and there are only so many of them.
என்னை நினை eṉṉai ninai — "think of me".
A bare verb stem is already a command — you met that with pō! in the farewell chapter — so this is a whole sentence with no machinery you have not used.

segments.text: What is me, as the one it is done to? (Eṉṉai.) And to me? (Enakku.) What do those two have in common? (The changed body eṉ-.) Which of the two endings would you put on it to say "for you"? (-உக்கு, on uṉ-.)

lessons.title: தேநீர் / தேநீரை (tēnīr / tēnīrai) — when the ending is a choice
lessons.gloss: the ending a person must have and a thing can do without — and the line Tamil draws where Spanish draws it too

segments.text: Say "I think of them". Say which piece of that sentence marks the one being thought of.
Now the part nobody tells you: that piece is not always required.

blocks.title: Grammar Lens: a person must have it, a thing need not

segments.text: அவரை நினைக்கிறேன் — I think of them தேநீர் வாங்குகிறேன் — I buy tea தேநீரை வாங்குகிறேன் — I buy the tea.
On a person the ending is obligatory. Leaving it off does not make a casual sentence; it makes a broken one.

On a thing it is a choice, and the choice carries meaning. Bare தேநீர் is tea in general, the kind of thing you buy. தேநீரை is that tea, a particular one already in view. Tamil has no word for the, and this is one of the places the job gets done instead.

utterances: the object is: a person. the ending: required.
the object is: a thing, in general. the ending: usually left off.
the object is: a thing, a particular one. the ending: put on.

blocks.title: Across the family: the same line, drawn at the other end

segments.text: Spanish draws this line too, and a Spanish learner has met it: veo la casa ("I see the house") against veo a María ("I see María"). A human object gets a marker; a thing does not.

Spanish puts that marker in front of the word as a separate piece. Tamil sticks it on the back. Same distinction between a person and a thing, opposite end of the word — which is the difference the dative chapter opened with, now showing up in a second place.

segments.text: When is -ஐ (-ai) obligatory? (When the object is a person.) What does putting it on a thing add? (That it is a particular one — Tamil has no word for the.) And where does Spanish put its marker for a human object? (In front, as a separate word, where Tamil puts it on the back.)

blocks.title: Grammar Lens: one ending, one question

utterances: the object: அவர் — that person. with the ending: அவரை. required?: yes.
the object: நான் — I. with the ending: என்னை. required?: yes.
the object: நீ — you. with the ending: உன்னை. required?: yes.
the object: தேநீர் — tea. with the ending: தேநீரை. required?: only for a particular one.

segments.text: Three of the four rows are people, and people have no choice. The question to ask of an object is not is this the subject or the object — the ending answers that — but is this a person.

Two things carry over from earlier chapters rather than being new here. The pronouns stand on the changed bodies eṉ- and uṉ- that the dative built. And the ending sits on the back of the word, which is what your first case ending taught and what separates this language from the one that would put a word in front.

segments.text: What is them, as the one it is done to? (Avarai.) What is me? (Eṉṉai.) When may the ending be left off? (On a thing, when it is not a particular one.) And what has to be true before it is compulsory? (The object is a person.)

lessons.title: (இவர், விடை, and the two we-words) (yār uḷḷē, yār veḷiyē) — one idea in four places
lessons.gloss: cold retrieval of four things the book said once, which turn out to be one idea — Tamil keeps track of who is present and who is included

segments.text: Introduce the person standing beside you as your friend.

blocks.title: Grammar Lens: the two words for we

utterances: word: நாம். who it covers: me, and you too.
word: நாங்கள். who it covers: me and my people, but not you.

segments.text: English has one we and leaves the listener guessing. Tamil makes you choose before you open your mouth, and the choice is audible to everyone in the room.
Getting it wrong is not a grammar slip — it either includes somebody you meant to exclude or shuts out somebody standing right there.

blocks.title: You'll want to know: இவர், and the ending that judges

segments.text: இவர் என் நண்பர் — this is my friend — is three words with no verb in the middle, the same silence the name sentence had.

What it adds is a choice of ending. நண்பர் carries respect; a plainer ending would not. Introducing someone in Tamil therefore states your regard for them out loud, in front of them, whether or not you meant to say anything about it.
விடை is leave to depart — a noun for the act of taking your leave, sharing a root with வீடு, the house.
Set it beside the farewells: the everyday one promises a return, and this word names the departure itself. Tamil has both, and it reserves the naming one for the heavier moment.
Page covered.

blocks.title: The exchange — five of them, unprompted

segments.text: The book opened with five, and an examiner opens with the same ones:
greet, and answer a thank-you.
trade names, both sides, closing warmly.
ask after the person, and reply in full.
take your leave, promising the next meeting.
say what you speak, and what you do.
